question: It takes \(A\) algebra books (all the same thickness) and \(H\) geometry books (all the same thickness, which is greater than that of an algebra book) to completely fill a certain shelf. Also, \(S\) of the algebra books and \(M\) of the geometry books would fill the same shelf. Finally, \(E\) of the algebra books alone would fill this shelf. Given that \(A,\) \(H,\) \(S,\) \(M,\) \(E\) are distinct positive integers, it follows that \(E\) is
solution:
Use the thickness of one algebra book as the unit of length, and let \(r>1\) be the thickness of a geometry book in these units. Since \(E\) algebra books fill the shelf, its length is \(E\) units. The two mixed arrangements therefore give
\[
A+Hr=E,\qquad S+Mr=E.
\]
We want \(E\), so eliminate the unknown thickness \(r\). Multiply the first equation by \(M\) and the second by \(H\):
\[
AM+HMr=ME,
\qquad SH+HMr=HE.
\]
Subtracting cancels the geometry-book contribution and gives
\[
AM-SH=(M-H)E.
\]
The integers \(M\) and \(H\) are distinct, so \(M-H\ne0\). Hence
\[
\boxed{E=\frac{AM-SH}{M-H}},
\]
choice \(\text{D}\).

edges.reason: After eliminating one unknown the procedure solves a one-variable linear equation; only this solving component is claimed.
Substitution seeks a pair satisfying both equations, so system and common-solution meanings are essential.
Substitution introduces the reduction-to-one-variable idea, but adding equations to cancel an unknown is justified independently by equality operations.
The reduction and back-substitution leave one-variable linear equations that must be solved; this is not a claim that every route must name transposition.
Adding/subtracting equations is performed to find their common solutions, not unrelated separate equation values.

edges.reason: A modeled two-equation system can be solved by addition/subtraction elimination instead of substitution; the optional method relation is correct.
Substitution can solve the modeled system without the addition/subtraction algorithm, so neither solving method should become a universal AND prerequisite.
